lessons.title: Rates of Reaction & Collision Theory
lessons.description: How collision theory, temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts control how fast reactions happen.
lessons.content_html:
What Controls How Fast a Reaction Happens?

Chemical reactions happen at different speeds. Some, like an explosion, are over in a fraction of a second. Others, like rusting, take months or years. The rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are converted into products. Understanding what affects this rate is a key part of the Edexcel specification.

Key Fact

For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with sufficient energy and in the correct orientation. The minimum energy needed for a successful collision is called the activation energy.

Collision Theory

Collision theory explains how reactions happen at the particle level. Reactant particles are constantly moving and colliding with each other. However, not every collision leads to a reaction. Only collisions where particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy — and where the particles are orientated correctly — result in a successful reaction.

The rate of reaction increases when:

  • The frequency of collisions increases (more collisions per second).
  • The energy of collisions increases (a greater proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy).

Factors Affecting the Rate of Reaction

Four main factors change the rate of a reaction. Each one works by changing either the frequency or the energy of particle collisions.

Increasing the temperature makes particles move faster. This has two effects: particles collide more frequently, and each collision carries more energy. A greater proportion of collisions now exceed the activation energy, so the rate increases significantly.

Increasing the concentration of a solution means there are more reactant particles in the same volume. They are closer together and collide more frequently, increasing the rate. For reactions involving gases, increasing the pressure has the same effect — the particles are pushed closer together, increasing collision frequency.

Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area to volume ratio. More particles on the surface are exposed to the other reactant, so collisions happen more often and the reaction is faster. Powdered marble chips react with acid much faster than large lumps of the same mass.

Catalysts

A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. It is not chemically changed and has the same mass at the end of the reaction. It does not alter the products formed.

A catalyst works by providing an alternative reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy. This means a greater proportion of particle collisions have enough energy to react, so the rate increases — even though the temperature has not changed.

Key Fact

A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering the activation energy. It provides an alternative pathway. The catalyst is unchanged chemically and unchanged in mass at the end of the reaction. It does not change the products.

Enzymes are biological catalysts found in living organisms. The specification notes that enzymes are used in the production of alcoholic drinks, where yeast enzymes catalyse the fermentation of sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Measuring the Rate of Reaction

The rate of a reaction can be determined experimentally by measuring how quickly a product is formed or a reactant is used up. Two common methods are:

  • Measuring gas production — collect gas in a gas syringe or measure loss of mass on a balance over time. For example, reacting hydrochloric acid with marble chips produces \(CO_2\) gas.
  • Observing a colour change — in the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, a yellow sulfur precipitate forms. The time taken for the solution to become opaque (a cross beneath the flask disappears) indicates the rate.

Graphs of mass, volume or concentration against time can be used to compare rates. A steeper gradient means a faster reaction. The gradient of the curve at any point gives the rate of reaction at that moment. As reactants are used up, the gradient decreases and the line levels off — the reaction is complete. Two curves on the same axes can show the effect of changing a variable (e.g. higher temperature gives a steeper initial gradient but the same final amount of product).

Key Fact

On a graph of volume of gas against time, the gradient (steepness) of the line represents the rate. A steeper line = faster rate. The line levels off when the reaction is complete and all the limiting reactant has been used up.

lessons.title: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium
lessons.description: How reversible reactions reach dynamic equilibrium, and the conditions used in the Haber process.
lessons.content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Most chemical reactions go to completion — reactants are fully converted into products and the reaction stops. However, some reactions are reversible. In a reversible reaction, the products can react together to re-form the original reactants. The reaction can go in both directions.

Reversible reactions are shown using the equilibrium symbol \(\rightleftharpoons\) instead of a normal arrow. For example, when ammonium chloride is heated it decomposes into ammonia and hydrogen chloride, but when the gases cool they recombine:

$$\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3(g) + \text{HCl}(g)$$

Key Fact

A reversible reaction can proceed in both the forward direction (reactants \(\rightarrow\) products) and the backward direction (products \(\rightarrow\) reactants). The \(\rightleftharpoons\) symbol shows this. The direction of some reversible reactions can be altered by changing the reaction conditions.

Hydrated copper sulfate is another example you may see in practicals. Blue hydrated copper sulfate turns white when heated (losing water), but adding water to the white anhydrous powder turns it blue again:

$$\text{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CuSO}_4(s) + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system (where no substances can enter or leave), it can reach a state of dynamic equilibrium.

At dynamic equilibrium:

  • The forward reaction and the backward reaction are both still happening.
  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but are not necessarily equal).
Key Fact

At dynamic equilibrium, both reactions are still taking place — it is not that the reactions have stopped. The word “dynamic” means the particles are still reacting in both directions. The word “equilibrium” means the rates are balanced, so there is no overall change in the amounts of reactants and products.

The Haber Process

The Haber process is an important industrial example of a reversible reaction. It produces ammonia from nitrogen (extracted from the air) and hydrogen (obtained from natural gas):

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

This reaction can reach dynamic equilibrium. The conditions used in the Haber process are a compromise chosen to give a reasonable yield at a reasonable rate:

The three conditions you need to recall are:

  • Temperature: 450 °C
  • Pressure: 200 atmospheres
  • Catalyst: Iron

The iron catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium — it speeds up both the forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster.

Changing the Position of Equilibrium

The position of equilibrium describes the relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium. If conditions change, the system shifts to counteract the change and establish a new equilibrium position.

If the forward reaction is exothermic, increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction (backwards), producing more reactants. Decreasing the temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction (forwards), producing more products. For the Haber process, the forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher yield of ammonia — but the rate would be too slow, hence the compromise of 450 °C.

Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas. In the Haber process, there are 4 moles of gas on the left (1 \(\text{N}_2\) + 3 \(\text{H}_2\)) and 2 moles on the right (2 \(\text{NH}_3\)). Higher pressure favours the forward reaction, increasing the yield of ammonia. This is why 200 atmospheres is used.

Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts the equilibrium towards the products (to the right), because the system acts to reduce the increased concentration by using it up. Increasing the concentration of a product shifts the equilibrium towards the reactants (to the left).

Key Fact

When conditions change, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Increasing concentration of a substance shifts equilibrium away from that substance.

lessons.title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons & Alkanes
lessons.description: What crude oil is, how fractional distillation separates it, and the properties of alkanes as a homologous series.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Crude Oil?

Crude oil is a naturally occurring mixture found deep underground. It formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient marine organisms buried under layers of sediment. Heat and pressure converted this organic matter into a complex mixture of hydrocarbons — compounds made of carbon and hydrogen atoms only.

Key Fact

Crude oil is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons. It contains molecules in which carbon atoms are joined in chains or rings. Crude oil is an important source of useful substances (fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry) and is a finite (non-renewable) resource.

Fractional Distillation

Crude oil is not useful as it comes out of the ground. It must be separated into simpler, more useful fractions by the process of fractional distillation.

In a fractionating column:

  • Crude oil is heated until most of it evaporates.
  • The vapour rises up the column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.
  • Hydrocarbons with high boiling points condense near the bottom; those with low boiling points rise further before condensing near the top.
  • Each fraction is collected at a different level.

You need to know the names and uses of these six fractions (from top to bottom of the column):

  • Gases (e.g. methane, propane, butane) — used in domestic heating and cooking.
  • Petrol — used as fuel for cars.
  • Kerosene — used as fuel for aircraft.
  • Diesel oil — used as fuel for some cars and trains.
  • Fuel oil — used as fuel for large ships and in some power stations.
  • Bitumen — used to surface roads and roofs.

How Fractions Differ

As you go down the fractionating column (from gases to bitumen), the hydrocarbon molecules get larger. This causes a pattern in their physical properties:

  • Number of carbon and hydrogen atoms increases (longer chains).
  • Boiling point increases (stronger intermolecular forces between larger molecules need more energy to overcome).
  • Viscosity increases (the liquid becomes thicker and harder to pour).
  • Ease of ignition decreases (larger molecules are harder to ignite).
Key Fact

Longer hydrocarbon molecules have higher boiling points, higher viscosity and are harder to ignite. Shorter molecules have lower boiling points, are less viscous and ignite more easily. This is because larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.

Alkanes — A Homologous Series

Most hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to a family called the alkanes. Alkanes are a homologous series — a family of compounds with a pattern. Every homologous series has four defining features:

  • They share the same general formula. For alkanes, this is \(C_nH_{2n+2}\).
  • Each member differs from the next by \(CH_2\) in their molecular formula.
  • They show a gradual variation in physical properties (e.g. boiling point increases steadily as chain length grows).
  • They have similar chemical properties because they share the same functional group (or in the case of alkanes, the same type of bonding).

Using the general formula \(C_nH_{2n+2}\):

  • Methane \(CH_4\) — 1 carbon. Found in natural gas.
  • Ethane \(C_2H_6\) — 2 carbons.
  • Propane \(C_3H_8\) — 3 carbons. Used in camping gas.
  • Butane \(C_4H_{10}\) — 4 carbons. Used in lighters.

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons — all carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds, so they contain the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.

Key Fact

Crude oil is a finite resource. Petrol, kerosene and diesel oil are non-renewable fossil fuels obtained from crude oil. Methane is a non-renewable fossil fuel found in natural gas. Once used, these cannot be replaced on a human timescale.

lessons.title: Combustion, Cracking & Alkenes
lessons.description: Complete and incomplete combustion, pollution from fossil fuels, and why cracking produces alkenes for polymers.
lessons.content_html:
Complete Combustion

Hydrocarbon fuels release energy when they burn. When there is a plentiful supply of oxygen, complete combustion occurs. The products are carbon dioxide and water, and energy is given out — the reaction is exothermic.

For example, the complete combustion of methane:

$$\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Key Fact

Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)) and water (\(H_2O\)). Energy is released (exothermic). This only happens when there is plenty of oxygen.

Incomplete Combustion

When the oxygen supply is limited, incomplete combustion occurs. Instead of all the carbon atoms forming carbon dioxide, some form carbon monoxide (\(CO\)) or carbon (soot). Water is still produced.

Incomplete combustion is a problem because:

  • Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas. It is colourless and odourless, so it cannot be detected without a detector. It binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, preventing them from carrying oxygen. This can be fatal.
  • Soot (carbon particles) causes breathing problems, contributes to smog, and blackens buildings.

Gas boilers, fires and cookers can produce carbon monoxide if they are faulty or poorly ventilated. Because carbon monoxide is colourless and has no smell, people may not realise it is present. Carbon monoxide detectors should be fitted in homes with gas appliances. Regular servicing ensures complete combustion and reduces the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.

Pollution from Burning Fuels

Burning hydrocarbon fuels causes several environmental problems beyond carbon monoxide and soot:

Some hydrocarbon fuels contain sulfur impurities. When these fuels burn, the sulfur reacts with oxygen to produce sulfur dioxide (\(SO_2\)). Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which damages buildings, kills aquatic life in lakes and rivers, and harms trees and other vegetation.

Inside car engines and power stations, the temperatures are extremely high. At these temperatures, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together to form oxides of nitrogen (\(NO_x\)). These gases also contribute to acid rain and can cause breathing problems. Note that the nitrogen comes from the air, not from the fuel.

Key Fact

Burning fossil fuels produces: \(CO_2\) (greenhouse gas, climate change), \(CO\) (toxic, binds to haemoglobin), soot (breathing problems), \(SO_2\) (acid rain from sulfur impurities), and \(NO_x\) (acid rain, formed at high temperatures from \(N_2\) and \(O_2\) in air).

Hydrogen as an Alternative Fuel

The specification asks you to evaluate hydrogen as an alternative to petrol for cars:

  • Advantages: The only product of burning hydrogen is water — no \(CO_2\), \(CO\), soot or \(SO_2\). It does not contribute to climate change or acid rain at the point of use.
  • Disadvantages: Hydrogen is difficult to store (it must be kept at very high pressure or very low temperature). It is highly flammable and explosive. Most hydrogen is currently produced from fossil fuels, which still releases \(CO_2\). Hydrogen fuel cells and filling stations are expensive and not widely available.

Cracking

Cracking is the process of breaking down larger, less useful hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones. It is carried out because the demand for short-chain hydrocarbons (like petrol and gases) is much greater than the supply from fractional distillation alone. There is a surplus of long-chain fractions (like fuel oil and bitumen).

Key Fact

Cracking is necessary because the supply of long-chain hydrocarbons from crude oil exceeds demand, while demand for short-chain hydrocarbons exceeds supply. Cracking produces shorter alkanes (saturated, for fuels) and alkenes (unsaturated, used to make polymers).

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons — they contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond (\(C=C\)). This makes them more reactive than alkanes. Alkenes are used as the starting material for making polymers (plastics) through polymerisation.

Cracking involves heating long-chain hydrocarbons to high temperatures and/or passing them over a catalyst. In the school practical, paraffin oil (a long-chain alkane mixture) is vaporised and passed over heated broken pottery (a catalyst). The products include shorter alkanes and alkenes. Alkenes can be tested for using bromine water — it turns from orange to colourless when an alkene is added, because the double bond reacts with bromine.

lessons.title: Polymers & Organic Reactions
lessons.description: Polymers, addition polymerisation, alkenes as monomers, polymer properties, uses, and environmental problems.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Polymers?

A polymer is a very large molecule made from many smaller molecules called monomers. These monomers bond together in long chains through a process called polymerisation. The most familiar example is poly(ethene), which is made from ethene monomers and used in everyday plastic products such as bags, bottles and packaging.

Key Fact

Polymers consist of large molecules containing long chains of carbon atoms. They are formed when many small monomer molecules join together in a polymerisation reaction.

Addition Polymerisation

Addition polymerisation occurs when unsaturated monomers, such as alkenes, open their carbon–carbon double bonds and join together. No other substance is produced — the only product is the polymer. For example, many ethene molecules join to form poly(ethene):

\(n\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2 \rightarrow -(\text{CH}_2\text{-CH}_2)_n\text{-}\)

The double bond in each ethene monomer breaks, and each carbon atom forms a new single bond with the next monomer in the chain. The ‘n’ in the equation represents a very large number of repeating units.

To draw a repeating unit of an addition polymer, take the monomer and remove the double bond. Replace it with single bonds extending from each carbon. Show bonds going out of each side of the brackets to indicate the chain continues. The repeating unit retains the same atoms as the monomer, just with single bonds instead of the double bond.

Alkenes — The Monomers for Addition Polymers

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons because they contain a carbon–carbon double bond (\(\text{C=C}\)). This double bond makes them reactive and able to undergo addition reactions. The general formula for alkenes is \(\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\). Common examples include ethene (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\)) and propene (\(\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\)).

Key Fact

Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond (\(\text{C=C}\)), making them unsaturated. This double bond allows them to undergo addition reactions, including addition polymerisation.

Testing for Alkenes

To test whether a hydrocarbon is an alkene, add bromine water. An alkene will decolourise bromine water, turning it from orange–brown to colourless. This happens because bromine adds across the double bond in an addition reaction. Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water because they have no double bond to react with.

Naming Addition Polymers

Addition polymers are named by placing the word ‘poly’ in front of the monomer name in brackets. Ethene becomes poly(ethene), propene becomes poly(propene), and chloroethene becomes poly(chloroethene) — better known by its common name PVC. The brackets around the monomer name are important because they distinguish the polymer from the monomer itself.

When you are given an unfamiliar polymer and asked to identify its monomer, reverse the process: take the repeating unit, replace the single bonds on each side with a double bond between the two carbon atoms, and you have the monomer. This skill is commonly tested in the exam.

Properties and Uses of Polymers

Different polymers have different properties depending on their monomer and structure. Poly(ethene) is flexible and waterproof, making it ideal for plastic bags and bottles. Poly(propene) is tougher and more heat-resistant, so it is used for food containers, ropes and carpets. Poly(chloroethene), commonly called PVC, is rigid and durable, widely used in window frames and pipes.

Not all polymers are synthetic. Natural polymers include DNA, starch, cellulose and proteins. DNA is a polymer made from nucleotide monomers. Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, but their different structures give them very different properties. Proteins are polymers of amino acids. These natural polymers are essential for life.

Problems with Polymers

Most synthetic polymers are not biodegradable. This means they persist in landfill sites and the natural environment for hundreds of years, causing pollution. Burning polymers can release toxic gases such as carbon monoxide, hydrogen chloride and hydrogen cyanide. Recycling helps reduce waste, but different polymer types must be separated first, which adds cost and complexity.

Key Fact

Most synthetic polymers are not biodegradable. They take hundreds of years to decompose in landfill and can release toxic gases when burned. Recycling reduces waste but requires sorting different polymer types.

Cracking breaks down larger, less useful hydrocarbon molecules from crude oil into smaller, more useful ones. This process produces alkenes, which are the monomers used in addition polymerisation. Without cracking, there would not be enough alkene monomers to meet the demand for plastic production. Cracking also produces shorter-chain alkanes that are in higher demand as fuels.

When asked to draw the repeating unit of a polymer, remember to remove the double bond from the monomer and extend single bonds out of each side of the bracket. Always include the ‘n’ subscript outside the bracket to show many units are joined.

Key Takeaways

  • Polymers are large molecules made from many small monomers joined by polymerisation.
  • Addition polymerisation uses alkene monomers — their double bonds open and join end-to-end with no other product.
  • Most synthetic polymers are not biodegradable, creating disposal challenges including pollution and toxic gases from incineration.

lessons.title: Chemical Analysis & Chromatography
lessons.description: Pure substances, mixtures, separation techniques, paper chromatography, Rf values, chemical gas tests, and potable water.
lessons.content_html:
Pure Substances and Mixtures

In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound that is not mixed with anything else. A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point and boiling point. A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically bonded. Mixtures melt and boil over a range of temperatures, which is how they can be distinguished from pure substances.

Key Fact

A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point. A mixture melts over a range of temperatures. Melting point data can therefore be used to check the purity of a substance.

Separation Techniques

Different mixtures require different separation methods, depending on the properties of the components. The main techniques are:

  • Filtration — separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel; the solid residue stays on the paper while the liquid filtrate passes through.
  • Crystallisation — used to obtain a dissolved solid (solute) from a solution. The solution is heated to evaporate some solvent, then left to cool so crystals form.
  • Simple distillation — separates a solvent from a solution. The solution is heated until the solvent evaporates, then the vapour is cooled and condensed in a condenser and collected as a pure liquid.
  • Fractional distillation — separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points. A fractionating column provides a temperature gradient so that each liquid condenses at a different height.

Paper Chromatography

Paper chromatography separates mixtures of soluble substances. A spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line near the bottom of chromatography paper. The paper is placed in a solvent (the mobile phase), which rises up the paper by capillary action. As the solvent moves through the mixture, different substances travel at different rates because they have different attractions to the paper (the stationary phase) and the solvent.

The result of paper chromatography is called a chromatogram. A pure substance produces a single spot. A mixture produces multiple spots, one for each component. You can identify unknown substances by comparing their spots with spots from known reference substances run alongside on the same chromatogram.

Rf Values

Each substance in a chromatogram can be identified by its Rf value. This is calculated using:

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$$

The Rf value is always between 0 and 1. It depends on the solvent used, so Rf values can only be compared when the same solvent and conditions are used. A substance with a higher Rf value is more soluble in the mobile phase and travels further up the paper.

Key Fact

Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front. Rf values are unique to each substance in a given solvent and can be used to identify unknown compounds.

In this core practical, spots of different inks are placed on chromatography paper along a pencil baseline. The paper is lowered into a beaker of solvent so the baseline is just above the solvent level. As the solvent rises, it separates the dyes in each ink. A pencil line (not pen) is used for the baseline because pencil is insoluble and will not dissolve in the solvent. The solvent front is marked with a pencil when the paper is removed, and Rf values are calculated for each spot.

Chemical Tests for Gases

Several important gases can be identified using simple chemical tests:

  • Oxygen — relights a glowing splint.
  • Hydrogen — burns with a squeaky pop when a lit splint is held near the mouth of a test tube.
  • Carbon dioxide — turns limewater milky (cloudy white).
  • Chlorine — bleaches damp litmus paper, turning it white.
Key Fact

Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white.

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not the same as pure water in chemistry — it contains low levels of dissolved substances. In the UK, potable water is produced from fresh water sources by sedimentation (letting solids settle), filtration (removing fine particles) and chlorination (killing bacteria). In areas without fresh water, sea water can be made potable by distillation or reverse osmosis, but these are energy-intensive processes.

Water used in chemical analysis must not contain any dissolved salts. This is because dissolved ions could interfere with test results, giving false positives or inaccurate measurements. Deionised or distilled water is used instead of tap water in laboratory analysis.

When answering questions about chromatography, always state both the mobile phase (solvent) and the stationary phase (paper). If asked to calculate Rf values, show your working clearly — divide the distance moved by the substance by the distance moved by the solvent front.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A pure substance has a sharp melting point; a mixture melts over a range.
  • Paper chromatography separates soluble substances using a mobile phase (solvent) and stationary phase (paper), and Rf values identify each substance.
  • Gas tests: oxygen relights a glowing splint, hydrogen gives a squeaky pop, CO\(_2\) turns limewater milky, chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.

lessons.title: Earth’s Atmosphere & Climate Change
lessons.description: How Earth's early atmosphere changed over billions of years to today's composition.
lessons.content_html:
Earth’s Early Atmosphere

Scientists believe the Earth’s early atmosphere was very different from today. It was formed by gases released during volcanic activity. The early atmosphere is thought to have contained a large amount of carbon dioxide, water vapour, and small amounts of other gases such as methane and ammonia. There was little or no oxygen.

Key Fact

The Earth’s early atmosphere was produced by volcanic activity. It contained mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with little or no oxygen.

How the Atmosphere Changed

Over billions of years, the atmosphere changed dramatically. As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the newly formed oceans, reducing its concentration in the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide was also locked up in sedimentary rocks such as limestone and in fossil fuels over millions of years.

The most important change came with the evolution of primitive plants and algae. These organisms carried out photosynthesis, absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and releasing oxygen. Over time, the level of oxygen gradually increased.

Carbon dioxide was also removed from the atmosphere by other processes. It dissolved in the oceans when they formed, and marine organisms used it to build shells and skeletons made of calcium carbonate. When these organisms died, their remains formed sedimentary rocks such as limestone and chalk. Carbon was also locked away in fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — formed from the remains of ancient organisms buried under layers of sediment over millions of years.

As oxygen levels rose, more complex organisms that depended on oxygen evolved. The build-up of oxygen also led to the formation of the ozone layer (\(\text{O}_3\)), which protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation. Today’s atmosphere contains approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and small amounts of other gases including about 0.04% carbon dioxide and varying amounts of water vapour.

Today’s Atmosphere

The composition of today’s atmosphere is approximately:

  • Nitrogen — about 78%
  • Oxygen — about 21%
  • Argon — about 0.9%
  • Carbon dioxide — about 0.04%
  • Plus small amounts of water vapour and other gases.
Key Fact

Today’s atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide.

The Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is a natural process that keeps the Earth warm enough to support life. Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. The warm surface then radiates longer-wavelength infrared radiation back towards space. Greenhouse gases — including carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour — absorb some of this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, warming the atmosphere.

Methane is produced by livestock farming, rice paddies and the decomposition of waste in landfill. Although present in much smaller quantities than carbon dioxide, methane is a more potent greenhouse gas — each molecule absorbs more infrared radiation than a molecule of carbon dioxide.

Climate Change

Climate change refers to long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns. Human activities — particularly burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) — have increased the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Livestock farming has increased methane levels. These increases enhance the greenhouse effect, leading to global warming.

Evidence for human-caused climate change includes the strong correlation between rising atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations, increased fossil fuel consumption and rising global temperatures over the past 150 years. However, scientists acknowledge uncertainties: measurements taken at different locations can vary, and historical data may be less accurate than modern records.

Key Fact

Burning fossil fuels increases atmospheric CO\(_2\). Livestock farming increases methane. Both enhance the greenhouse effect and contribute to global warming and climate change.

The potential effects of increased global temperatures include: rising sea levels due to thermal expansion of water and melting ice caps; more frequent and severe extreme weather events such as floods, droughts and storms; changes in habitats and biodiversity, with some species unable to adapt quickly enough; and disruption to agriculture and food supplies. Mitigation measures include reducing fossil fuel use, increasing renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, and carbon capture and storage technologies.

Testing for Oxygen

The chemical test for oxygen is to place a glowing splint into the gas. If oxygen is present, the splint relights. This test was historically important in establishing that photosynthesis produces oxygen.

When evaluating evidence for climate change, always discuss both the correlation between CO\(_2\) levels, fossil fuel use and temperature, and the uncertainties in the data. The exam expects you to weigh the evidence rather than simply state that climate change is happening.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The early atmosphere was mainly CO\(_2\) and water vapour from volcanoes, with little oxygen. Photosynthesis by early plants gradually increased oxygen and decreased CO\(_2\).
  • Greenhouse gases (CO\(_2\), methane, water vapour) absorb infrared radiation from the Earth and re-emit it, keeping the planet warm.
  • Human activities — burning fossil fuels and livestock farming — have increased greenhouse gas levels, causing climate change. Evidence includes correlations between CO\(_2\), fossil fuel use and temperature rise.

lessons.title: Using Resources & Life Cycle Assessment
lessons.description: Finite and renewable resources, metal recycling, life cycle assessment, and sustainable resource use.
lessons.content_html:
Finite and Renewable Resources

The resources we use come from the Earth’s crust, oceans and atmosphere. Some resources are finite (non-renewable) — they are being used faster than they can be replaced. Fossil fuels, metal ores and minerals are all finite resources. Other resources are renewable, meaning they can be replenished, such as timber from managed forests or crops.

Key Fact

Finite resources (such as crude oil and metal ores) are being used up and cannot be replaced. Renewable resources (such as timber and crops) can be replenished.

Recycling Metals

Metals are extracted from ores found in the Earth’s crust. Extracting metals from their ores requires large amounts of energy and has significant environmental impacts, including mining damage to landscapes, noise, dust, and loss of habitats. Recycling metals offers several advantages over extracting new metal from ore.

Recycling metals uses less energy than extracting metals from ores, which reduces carbon dioxide emissions and saves money. It conserves finite resources by reducing the amount of ore that needs to be mined. It also reduces the amount of waste going to landfill and reduces the environmental damage caused by mining operations. However, metals must be sorted and cleaned before recycling, which adds cost and complexity.

What Is a Life Cycle Assessment?

A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product throughout its entire life — from raw material extraction to final disposal. The four key stages are:

  1. Extracting and processing raw materials — mining ores, drilling for oil, growing crops. This often involves energy use, habitat destruction and pollution.
  2. Manufacturing and packaging — turning raw materials into products. This requires energy (often from fossil fuels), produces waste, and may use water and chemicals.
  3. Use and operation — the energy and resources consumed while the product is being used. For example, a car uses fuel and produces exhaust emissions throughout its life.
  4. Disposal — what happens at the end of the product’s useful life. Options include landfill, incineration, or recycling. Each has different environmental consequences.
Key Fact

A life cycle assessment considers the environmental impact at four stages: extracting raw materials, manufacturing, use, and disposal. It helps companies and consumers make more sustainable choices.

Life cycle assessments can be difficult to carry out accurately. Some environmental impacts are hard to quantify — for example, how do you measure the value of lost biodiversity or visual pollution? Different assessors may also give different weightings to different impacts, introducing bias. Companies may selectively present LCA data to make their products look more environmentally friendly than they really are, a practice sometimes called greenwashing.

The Use and Disposal Stages

The ‘use’ stage of a product’s life can have a larger environmental impact than its manufacture. A car, for example, burns fuel and produces exhaust emissions throughout its entire working life — far more CO\(_2\) than was released during its construction. Electrical products consume energy from the grid, which may come from fossil fuel power stations. The disposal stage also matters: landfill takes up space and can pollute groundwater, incineration releases CO\(_2\) and potentially toxic gases, while recycling requires energy for collection and reprocessing but avoids the need for new raw materials.

Reducing the Use of Resources

There are three main strategies for reducing the impact on finite resources, often called the “three Rs”:

  • Reduce — use fewer resources in the first place. For example, using less packaging or making products that last longer.
  • Reuse — use items again instead of throwing them away. Glass bottles can be collected, washed and refilled.
  • Recycle — collect and reprocess materials to make new products. Metals, glass, paper and some plastics can be recycled.

Phytoextraction uses plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil. The plants are then harvested and burned, and the metals are extracted from the ash. Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds from low-grade ores. Both methods are slower than traditional mining but have lower environmental impact and can extract metals from ores that would otherwise be uneconomic to mine.

Key Fact

Recycling metals uses less energy, reduces CO\(_2\) emissions, conserves finite ore reserves and reduces landfill waste compared to extracting new metals from ores.

Using Resources Sustainably

Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the current generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Chemistry plays a key role through developing new materials, improving recycling processes, and finding ways to use renewable resources instead of finite ones.

When evaluating a life cycle assessment, consider all four stages and think about which stages have the greatest environmental impact for that particular product. Remember that some impacts are subjective and difficult to quantify, which is a limitation of LCAs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Finite resources like fossil fuels and metal ores are being used up; renewable resources can be replenished.
  • A life cycle assessment evaluates a product’s environmental impact across four stages: raw materials, manufacturing, use and disposal.
  • Recycling metals saves energy, reduces emissions and conserves finite resources. Reduce, reuse and recycle are key strategies for sustainability.
